feedback: If a learner treats dinosaur grouping as settled, point to the 2017 Ornithoscelida proposal as an example of the traditional split being actively challenged.
A good explanation notes that classifications are inferences from anatomical evidence and can be revised when that evidence is reinterpreted.
activities.intendedInsight: A classification is a hypothesis built from evidence, not a fixed fact; scientists actively debate and revise how dinosaurs are grouped.
learnerActions: Read or listen to a short account of why the two-group scheme was proposed and why a 2017 study (the Ornithoscelida hypothesis, Baron, Norman & Barrett) proposed reorganising it.
Compare a simple before/after family-tree sketch showing the traditional split and the proposed rearrangement.
Explain in one or two sentences why even a long-established classification can change when new evidence is weighed.
activities.title: Why the family tree was re-argued

feedback: Birds evolved from the LIZARD-hipped theropods (Saurischia), not the bird-hipped group. This surprises people because a bird's own pubis points backward (bird-shaped), yet that backward pubis evolved separately (convergently) — so by ancestry a bird is a lizard-hipped theropod. The group names describe the hip anatomy of the dinosaur groups, and 'bird-hipped' does not mark the bird ancestors.
The deciding feature is the pubis direction; diet and size do not determine the group, which is why carnivorous theropods and herbivorous sauropods are both lizard-hipped.
T. rex and Brachiosaurus share the forward/down pubis, so both are Saurischia despite looking very different.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding is shown by correctly classifying by hip structure AND explaining that the group names describe pelvis anatomy, not bird ancestry or diet.
learnerActions: Answer: which group did birds evolve from — lizard-hipped or bird-hipped — and why is that surprising?
Sort several named species into Saurischia and Ornithischia.
Answer: what single feature do you look at to decide a dinosaur's group?
Explain: T. rex (a fierce meat-eater) and Brachiosaurus (a gentle long-neck) are in the SAME hip group — how can that be?
activities.title: Check: naming trap and the sorting rule
